lesson.title: Fire or Don't: The Rule Behind Every Neural Signal
lesson.summary: The all-or-none principle states that once a neuron's membrane potential crosses threshold it fires a full, uniform action potential, so stimulus intensity is encoded through firing rate and the number of neurons recruited rather than the size of individual signals.
lesson.body:
Neurons follow a strict rule when it comes to generating an electrical signal, known as the all-or-none principle. Once the electrical charge inside a neuron reaches a critical threshold, the neuron fires a full action potential, a spike of electrical activity that travels the entire length of the axon at essentially the same size and speed every time. If the incoming signal never reaches that threshold, no action potential fires at all, not a smaller or weaker version of one. There is no in-between state.

A useful comparison is a gun trigger. Squeeze it just past the point of resistance and the gun fires with the same force every time, whether you squeezed gently past that point or yanked it hard. Squeeze less than that and nothing happens at all, no matter how close you got. The neuron behaves the same way: crossing threshold produces a full, uniform action potential, and falling short produces nothing.

One consequence of this rule is the refractory period, a brief window immediately after an action potential fires during which that section of the neuron cannot fire again, or can only do so with a much stronger stimulus. This built-in recovery time places an upper limit on how rapidly a neuron can fire repeatedly, and it also helps ensure that an action potential travels in only one direction down the axon, since the stretch of membrane that just fired is temporarily unable to fire again behind it.

This creates an interesting puzzle. If every action potential in a given neuron is the same size, how does the nervous system represent the difference between a light touch and a firm press, or a dim light and a bright one? The answer is that intensity is encoded not in the size of any single action potential, but in the rate at which a neuron fires and in how many neurons are recruited to fire at once. A strong stimulus causes affected neurons to fire more rapidly and activates a larger number of neurons, while a weak stimulus produces slower firing in fewer neurons, even though every individual spike involved is identical in size.

This is why a light touch on your skin and a firm press feel different even though the sensory neurons involved obey the same all-or-none rule. The firm press pushes more sensory neurons past threshold and drives the ones that do fire to fire more rapidly in quick succession, and it is this pattern of frequency and recruitment, not the strength of any one impulse, that your brain interprets as greater intensity.

The all-or-none principle applies broadly, to the sensory neurons that detect stimuli, the motor neurons that trigger muscle contraction, and the interneurons that process information in between. It is worth noting that not every electrical change in a neuron is all-or-none: small, graded changes in voltage occur constantly at the dendrites and cell body as inputs are summed together, and only when that summed activity crosses threshold does the full, uniform action potential fire and propagate down the axon.
